checks: The linearly interpolated radii are concave: the successive slopes are reversed nonnegative drops, zero, then forward negatives. The resulting hypograph in the nonnegative continuous quadrant is compact, convex and has interior on the central slab. Its integer bases are exactly −m,…,m+1; summing all paired planar areas gives 2VW. Point fibers have zero area whether included or not.

Tightening a closed halfspace to y reduces its mass. A pure base normal includes at least one whole fiber per pair, including the through-base-zero boundary. With a nonzero continuous normal, the barycentric swap has absolute determinant one on each positive-radius triangle. It changes the through-y comparison margin by vᵢ(R−r)≤0, leaving a single ambient minorant cap with w≥0 and positive coordinate sum; zero fibers need no change of variables.

At bases −h and h+1, the thresholds with tilt +β are t+βh and t−β(h+1); with −β they are t−βh and t+β(h+1). Subtracting in that order gives the two nonnegative differences in the proof. This handles all real tilts including zero, preserving the prescribed y and same normal in the low-sector statement.

The accepted high-normal theorem applies at d=2 and M=a≥2/3 with Γ₂=4/9. For the separate strengthened low-sector claim, the affine predecessor compares the per-pair signed surpluses with the same R, u and β, not the two raw masses. The own pair pays at least R²/18 in units of V for every β and covers m=0.

When β≥α/3, each positive-radius left fiber contains its own centroid since t−βh≤ℓₕ/3, including α=0 and equality. Ordinary triangle centroid depth pays (4/9)ℓₕ². Zero-radius fibers contribute zero; the retained own bonus pays the required R²/162.

When β<α/3, scaling by R gives 0<k≤1 and 0≤β<k/3; each positive radius has qₕ≥rₕ/3>0 and pₕ≥rₕ/3>0. For r/3≤q<r/2 the three barycentrics at (q,q) have maximum at most 1/2 and the first coordinate is a smallest coordinate. The central simplex depth formula therefore gives 4q(r−2q) in units of V. For q≥r/2 the positive-part bound is zero. Zero radii are excluded from the kernel, and the own envelope at h=0 is 4/9 before adding the bonus once.

Independently evaluated both d=2 knots of the accepted maximum formula. At H=1, k=2/3, positive radii are 1 and 1/3, so W=10/9 and K=1. At H=2, k=1/2, the positive radii are 1 and 1/2 (the next radius is zero), and W=K=5/4. The maximal deficit is (4/9)(1/9)=4/81; 1/18−4/81=1/162. Exact rational spot checks confirmed these values.

The two ratio derivatives have positive numerators k/3−β and β+k(1/3+β). Cap tails need only be nonincreasing, so normalized surpluses are weakly nonincreasing. The last positive radius exists since r₀=1. If its normalized surplus is nonnegative (including equality), every earlier outer pair is nonnegative, giving the own bonus. If it is negative, every appended positive term is negative, so removing the suffix can only increase the full-leg surplus. A terminal zero radius contributes zero; extension stays on integer indices. Scaling back and the pointwise comparison transfer the full additive bound to the original chain.

At m=0 and β≥2R/3 the sharpness cap has normalized base-zero area (R−R/3)²=(4/9)R²; the other fiber is null in the cap, even at its supporting endpoint. The ratio is 2/9. In fact this same two-fiber example cannot have greater maximum depth: any point is in one fiber, where the ordinary depth is at most 4/9 by the two smallest barycentric coordinates, and a sufficiently steep tilt isolates that cap from the other fiber.
